    App chạy foreground: Chat và call có thể hoạt động tốt nếu triển khai WebRTC đúng cách.

    App xuống background: Android có thể hạn chế hoặc tạm dừng WebView, khiến cuộc gọi bị gián đoạn. Tauri có tài liệu về giới hạn background throttling.

Được\! Và mình nghĩ có thể làm một dự án khá hay: Mini Zalo – ứng dụng nhắn tin riêng tư, tự chọn nơi lưu dữ liệu, chạy đa nền tảng.

Mục tiêu là một ứng dụng kiểu Zalo/WhatsApp thu nhỏ, nhưng có điểm khác biệt: người dùng tự quyết định dữ liệu nằm ở đâu. Không bắt buộc tất cả phải lưu trên server của bạn.

Mình đề xuất thiết kế theo kiểu Local-first + Multi-storage + Self-hosted.

## 2\. Người dùng tự chọn nơi lưu dữ liệu

Đây là phần mình thích nhất trong ý tưởng của bạn.

1\. Lưu trực tiếp trên điện thoại / máy tính

Local

- Tin nhắn và danh bạ lưu trong SQLite.
- File ảnh/video lưu trên máy.
- Không cần thuê server.
- Có thể dùng offline.
- Nếu mất máy mà chưa backup thì có nguy cơ mất dữ liệu.

2\. Google Drive

Cloud backup

- Backup tin nhắn, hình ảnh, file.
- Khôi phục khi đổi điện thoại.
- Đồng bộ dữ liệu giữa các thiết bị qua cơ chế riêng.

Lưu ý: Google Drive nên dùng để backup/restore, không nên dùng như database chat trực tiếp vì dễ phát sinh xung đột khi nhiều thiết bị cùng ghi dữ liệu.

3\. NAS / ổ cứng mạng

Private storage

- Synology, QNAP hoặc NAS tự dựng.
- Lưu ảnh, video, tài liệu.
- Có thể chạy server riêng bằng Docker.
- Truy cập từ điện thoại và máy tính khi ở ngoài nhà.

4\. Server riêng – Big Boss

Enterprise

- Mỗi người có tài khoản riêng.
- Đồng bộ tin nhắn theo thời gian thực.
- Quản lý nhóm, phân quyền, nhiều thiết bị.
- Mở rộng hàng nghìn hoặc nhiều người dùng hơn tùy cấu hình.
- Tự quản lý dữ liệu và hạ tầng.

Điểm quan trọng: Không cần chọn một nơi lưu duy nhất cho toàn bộ ứng dụng. Có thể lưu tin nhắn trong database, file trên NAS, backup lên Google Drive và đồng bộ qua server. Người dùng được chọn cấu hình phù hợp.

Một lời khuyên: Hãy làm một codebase Flutter duy nhất, thiết kế storage adapter ngay từ đầu. Sau này người dùng cá nhân dùng miễn phí, người có NAS tự lưu, còn Big Boss có thể thuê hoặc tự vận hành server riêng. iOS cần thêm máy Mac/Xcode để build và ký ứng dụng iPhone.

Mục tiêu là một Mini Zalo mà bạn sở hữu mã nguồn và có thể tự triển khai, không bị khóa vào một nhà cung cấp cloud nào.


Đúng rồi. Mình sẽ thiết kế Mini Zalo theo nguyên tắc người dùng toàn quyền chọn nơi lưu dữ liệu và nơi backup dữ liệu, hai chức năng này độc lập hoàn toàn với nhau.

Ví dụ: lưu tin nhắn trên điện thoại nhưng backup lên NAS, hoặc lưu trên server nhưng backup sang Google Drive.

BackupCho phép chọn một hoặc nhiều nơi khác với nơi lưu chính.

## 3. Những chức năng cần có

- Tự động backup theo giờ, ngày hoặc tuần.
- Backup khi có Wi-Fi.
- Backup chỉ khi đang sạc.
- Backup thủ công.
- Khôi phục dữ liệu trên thiết bị mới.
- Kiểm tra dung lượng và trạng thái backup.
- Mã hóa bản backup bằng mật khẩu hoặc khóa riêng.
- Kiểm tra tính toàn vẹn dữ liệu.
- Chuyển nơi lưu mà không mất lịch sử chat.
- Xuất dữ liệu để không bị phụ thuộc vào ứng dụng.

Một điểm kỹ thuật quan trọng: Đường link ổ cứng cần hỗ trợ đúng giao thức như SMB, WebDAV, SFTP hoặc S3. Không phải URL nào cũng có thể dùng làm ổ lưu trữ. Trên iOS và Android, quyền truy cập file cũng có giới hạn riêng.

## 5. Mình muốn bổ sung một nguyên tắc rất quan trọng

Không khóa dữ liệu vào Mini Zalo.

Người dùng có thể:

- Đổi điện thoại nhưng giữ nguyên lịch sử.
- Chuyển từ Google Drive sang NAS.
- Chuyển từ NAS lên server riêng.
- Xuất toàn bộ tin nhắn, hình ảnh, file.
- Rời ứng dụng nhưng vẫn giữ dữ liệu của mình.

Mình sẽ đưa nguyên tắc này vào kiến trúc kỹ thuật ngay từ đầu.

Đề xuất thêm: Cho phép chọn nhiều nơi lưu chính và thiết lập ưu tiên, ví dụ Local là chính, NAS là bản đồng bộ, Google Drive là bản backup. Khi một nơi mất kết nối, ứng dụng vẫn hoạt động và đồng bộ lại khi kết nối phục hồi.


Nếu viết riêng Kotlin cho Android và Swift cho iOS, mình đánh giá đây là phương án rất tốt cho Mini Zalo, đặc biệt vì dự án của bạn có yêu cầu lưu trữ linh hoạt: điện thoại, Google Drive, NAS, ổ cứng mạng và server riêng.

Thay vì cố gắng dùng một codebase cho tất cả, chúng ta xây dựng hai ứng dụng native riêng, nhưng dùng chung backend, giao thức, database schema và quy tắc đồng bộ.

Mình gọi kiến trúc này là Native Multi-Platform + Shared Backend.

# 3. Hệ thống lưu trữ đa lựa chọn

Đây là phần quan trọng nhất của Mini Zalo.

Mình sẽ thiết kế Storage Adapter để Android và iOS có cùng một giao thức lưu trữ, nhưng mỗi nền tảng có implementation riêng.

## Storage Manager

Storage Interface

Giao diện thống nhất cho mọi loại lưu trữ

Local Storage

SQLite, file nội bộ

Google Drive

Cloud API

NAS

SMB, WebDAV, SFTP

Private Server

S3, HTTPS API

Ví dụ cấu hình:

| Dữ liệu chính | Backup |
| --- | --- |
| Android | Google Drive |
| iPhone | NAS |
| Windows | Ổ cứng ngoài |
| Server | NAS thứ hai |
| NAS | Google Drive |

Một số giới hạn cần xử lý:

- iOS không cho ứng dụng tự do truy cập toàn bộ ổ cứng; phải thông qua Files và quyền được cấp.
- Android dùng Storage Access Framework để người dùng cấp quyền thư mục.
- NAS cần giao thức mạng thích hợp; SMB không được hỗ trợ trực tiếp giống nhau trên mọi nền tảng.
- Google Drive cần OAuth và quản lý token an toàn.
- Backup phải có versioning, kiểm tra checksum và cơ chế khôi phục.

# 4. Backend dùng chung cho cả hai app

Mình đề xuất Node.js + TypeScript cho backend.

| Service | Nhiệm vụ |
| --- | --- |
| Auth | Đăng nhập, đăng ký, phiên đăng nhập |
| User | Hồ sơ, avatar, danh bạ |
| Chat | Tin nhắn riêng và nhóm |
| Realtime | WebSocket |
| Media | Ảnh, video, file |
| Storage | Quản lý các nơi lưu |
| Backup | Lập lịch, backup, restore |
| Sync | Đồng bộ nhiều thiết bị |
| Notification | Push notification |

Database:

- PostgreSQL: dữ liệu tài khoản, nhóm, metadata.
- SQLite: dữ liệu local từng thiết bị.
- Redis: cache, presence và hàng đợi khi cần.
- S3/MinIO: lưu file và media.

Với E2EE, nội dung tin nhắn được mã hóa ở thiết bị trước khi gửi; server chỉ lưu ciphertext và metadata tối thiểu cần thiết.

# 6. Còn Windows và Linux thì sao?

Vì bạn muốn ứng dụng chạy cả Windows và Linux, mình đề xuất có thêm desktop client sau:

- Windows: Kotlin Multiplatform Desktop hoặc Tauri.
- Linux: Tauri hoặc Kotlin Multiplatform Desktop.
- Web: React nếu cần truy cập qua trình duyệt.

Tất cả dùng chung API và protocol với Android/iOS.

Không cần phát triển cả năm nền tảng cùng một lúc.

# 7. Lộ trình phát triển mình đề xuất

1. Giai đoạn 1 – Core Platform
   Thiết kế database, API, authentication, storage adapter và giao thức đồng bộ.
2. Giai đoạn 2 – Android Kotlin
   Chat 1-1, nhóm, gửi file, local storage và backup.
3. Giai đoạn 3 – iOS Swift
   Xây dựng app native tương thích API, đồng bộ và E2EE.
4. Giai đoạn 4 – Desktop
   Windows, Linux, quản lý file và NAS.
5. Giai đoạn 5 – Big Boss
   Self-hosted server, multi-tenant, quản trị, mở rộng và monitoring.

# 8\. Có một quyết định kiến trúc cần chốt

Theo mình có hai kiểu sản phẩm khác nhau:

A. Mini Zalo độc lập (khuyên dùng)

- Người dùng tự tạo tài khoản Mini Zalo.
- Có server mặc định nhưng không bắt buộc dùng server của bạn.
- Có thể tự host server riêng.
- Có thể sử dụng hoàn toàn local cho những tính năng phù hợp.
- Người dùng chọn nơi lưu và backup độc lập.

B. Mini Zalo P2P / Decentralized

- Các thiết bị kết nối trực tiếp khi có thể.
- Không phụ thuộc một server trung tâm cho mọi hoạt động.
- NAS hoặc máy tính cá nhân có thể làm node.
- Phức tạp hơn về NAT traversal, offline delivery, đồng bộ và quản lý khóa.

1\. Kiến trúc hệ thống

hybrid A. Hybrid – Server + Local + NAS + Cloud

B. P2P – Ưu tiên kết nối trực tiếp

C. Cả hai – hỗ trợ cả Hybrid và P2P

# 2. Gradle là gì?

Bạn hỏi rất đúng. Mình giải thích đơn giản nhé.

Hãy tưởng tượng bạn đang xây một căn nhà:

| Công cụ | Vai trò |
| --- | --- |
| Android Studio | Xưởng làm việc |
| Kotlin | Ngôn ngữ xây dựng |
| Gradle | Quản lý quá trình xây dựng |
| Android SDK | Bộ công cụ Android |
| OpenCode | Trợ lý AI viết code |
| Room | Quản lý database |
| APK | Sản phẩm cài đặt lên điện thoại |

Gradle không phải ngôn ngữ lập trình.

Gradle là hệ thống Build Automation, chịu trách nhiệm:

- Tải và quản lý thư viện cần thiết.
- Biên dịch Kotlin.
- Xây dựng các module.
- Chạy kiểm thử.
- Đóng gói APK/AAB.
- Quản lý cấu hình build.

Ví dụ khi chạy:

powershell

```powershell
.\gradlew assembleDebug
```

Gradle sẽ xây dựng ứng dụng Android và tạo file APK debug.

# 6. Bây giờ kiểm tra máy trước khi tạo project

Vì bạn đã cài Android Studio, OpenCode/FreeCode và Gradle rồi, chúng ta không cần tải lại hoặc cài lại một cách mù quáng.

Mở PowerShell và chạy lần lượt đoạn sau. Đây chỉ là lệnh kiểm tra, không xóa hay sửa dữ liệu.

powershell

```powershell

Write-Host "===== KONNEX ENVIRONMENT CHECK =====" -ForegroundColor Cyan

Write-Host "`n[1] Java"
java -version

Write-Host "`n[2] Gradle"
gradle -v

Write-Host "`n[3] Android SDK"
Write-Host "ANDROID_HOME=$env:ANDROID_HOME"
Write-Host "ANDROID_SDK_ROOT=$env:ANDROID_SDK_ROOT"

Write-Host "`n[4] Kotlin"
if (Get-Command kotlinc -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
    kotlinc -version
} else {
    Write-Host "Kotlin CLI not found (may be managed by Gradle)"
}

Write-Host "`n[5] OpenCode"
if (Get-Command opencode -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
    opencode --version
} else {
    Write-Host "OpenCode command not found"
}

Write-Host "`n[6] FreeCode"
if (Get-Command freecode -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue) {
    freecode --version
} else {
    Write-Host "FreeCode command not found"
}

Write-Host "`n[7] Disk space"
Get-PSDrive -PSProvider FileSystem |
    Select-Object Name,
    @{Name="FreeGB";Expression={[math]::Round($_.Free/1GB,2)}},
    @{Name="UsedGB";Expression={[math]::Round($_.Used/1GB,2)}}

Write-Host "`n[8] Project folder"
Test-Path "D:\AI\appDevelopment\7miniChatCall"
```

Sau khi chạy, gửi mình kết quả PowerShell.

Mình sẽ dựa vào đúng môi trường máy bạn để viết cấu hình Gradle, Android SDK và OpenCode. Không bắt bạn cài lại những gì đã có.

Mục tiêu bước tiếp theo: tạo được project KONNEX đầu tiên trên ổ D, mở thành công bằng Android Studio và build được APK debug. Sau đó mới giao từng module cho OpenCode thực hiện. :))

### 2. Modules implemented (34, from `settings.gradle.kts`)

- **`:app`** — composition root (`AppContainer`), single NavHost, bottom bar, Application, manifest.
- **Core (7):** `core:common` (Outcome/typed errors, clock, ids, SHA-256, logger), `core:model`, `core:database` (Room, 9 tables, DAOs, transactions), `core:network` (Ktor client + API DTOs), `core:security` (Keystore AES-256-GCM, encrypted secret store, security report), `core:designsystem` (original palette/type/components/Canvas logo), `core:testing`.
- **Domain (7, pure JVM):** auth, messaging, contacts, storage, backup (archive format + manifest), sync (merge policy/planner), calling (reducer).

VT-x was enabled but no hypervisor existed, so I installed the Android Emulator Hypervisor Driver (`aehd` 2.2) from the SDK — this required your admin approval, which you granted. `emulator -accel-check` now reports *"AEHD (version 2.2) is installed and usable"*. **No physical phone was touched**; `ANDROID_SERIAL=emulator-5554` pinned the run to the emulator.

**Instrumentation results — 8/8 passed** (`:app:connectedDebugAndroidTest`, BUILD SUCCESSFUL):

```
AppStartupTest.applicationCreatesContainerAndMainActivityResumes
DatabasePersistenceTest.opensEveryTableAndPersistsAMessage
DatabasePersistenceTest.syncCursorSurvivesUpdatesAndNeverRegressesLocally
KeystoreStorageTest.cipherRoundTripUsesAKeystoreKey
KeystoreStorageTest.secretStoreEncryptsAtRestAndRemovesKeys
OutboxTransactionTest.creatingAConversationQueuesOneConversationChange
OutboxTransactionTest.sendingAMessageWritesMessagePreviewAndOutbox
OutboxTransactionTest.deletingAMessageWritesATombstoneWhenItWasSent
```

Two real failures were found and fixed, not worked around: a `ConversationEntity` constructor mismatch, and a genuine one — the Keystore test created a second `SecureSecretStore` over the same DataStore file, which fails by design ("multiple DataStores active for the same file"). The test now reuses the app's process-wide store, which is what production does; it also asserts the plaintext secret never appears in the on-disk preferences file.

### Phase 2 — Automatic sync

`SyncCoordinator` (`:sync`) decides *when*; `SyncEngine` still decides *what*.

- **After sign-in**: `AuthenticationRoute`'s continue callback triggers an immediate run and starts periodic work (only when a server session exists).
- **Foreground**: `ProcessLifecycleOwner.onStart` in `KonnexApplication`.
- **Connectivity recovery**: `registerDefaultNetworkCallback.onAvailable`.
- **Periodic**: WorkManager `konnex-sync`, 15-minute minimum, `CONNECTED`, exponential backoff from 30 s.
- **Battery discipline**: single-flight, one run per 20 s for automatic triggers (`SyncPolicy`, unit-tested), retries only for `Network`/`RateLimited` at 5 s → 15 s → 45 s then stop; no timers, no polling. A dead session (`Unauthorized`) is a terminal result, not a retry loop.
- Cursor persistence and duplicate-safe delivery unchanged and covered by existing tests; Settings still shows the live sync pill, last-sync time and queued count.

### Phase 3 — Token refresh

- `POST /v1/auth/refresh` with **atomic single-use rotation**: the presented refresh hash is part of the `UPDATE … WHERE`, so a replay or the loser of a concurrent pair gets 401; the old access token dies in the same statement. Access tokens now default to **60 minutes**; refresh lifetime 30 days, sliding.
- Client refreshes 2 minutes before expiry and once on any 401 (never in a loop), serialised by a mutex plus a generation check. A rejected refresh deletes the tokens and reports "Your session expired. Sign in again."
- Store: `sessionByRefreshHash` + `rotateSession`, migration **v2** (`idx_sessions_refresh`), per-IP refresh limiter.
- **Tests**: 6 server tests (`AuthRefreshTest`) and 4 client tests (refresh body/path, 401→refresh→retry with new token, rejected refresh not looped, no refresher = single attempt). Live check against a running server: 60.0-minute TTL, old access 401 after rotation, new access 200, replayed refresh 401, chained rotation 200, refresh after revoke 401.

### Phase 4 — Regression (all executed)

| Command | Result |
|---|---|
| `./gradlew :app:assembleDebug test` | **BUILD SUCCESSFUL** — 90 Android unit tests, 0 failures |
| `./gradlew -p server test` | **BUILD SUCCESSFUL** — 35 tests, 0 failures |
| `./gradlew :app:compileDebugAndroidTestKotlin` | **BUILD SUCCESSFUL** |
| `ANDROID_SERIAL=emulator-5554 ./gradlew :app:connectedDebugAndroidTest` | **8/8 passed** |

**APK**: `app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk` — 20,075,490 bytes (19.1 MiB), installed on the emulator during the run.

### Phase 5 — Documentation & commit

Updated `README.md`, `ROADMAP.md`, `SECURITY.md`, `SYNC_ENGINE.md`, `API_SPEC.md`, `server/README.md` (new endpoint, 60-minute TTL, scheduling rules, honest UI text that no longer claims rotation is missing). Documentation duties from `AGENTS.md` are covered for API, security and sync.

Committed as **`7f88a9d`** — *"Validate on an API 35 emulator and make sync automatic with token refresh"*; working tree is clean.

### Remaining limitations

1. **Two-device delivery is still unverified.** One emulator exists; I did not install on your two physical phones. Protocol-level two-client tests pass, plus the live HTTP run.
2. Sync is event-driven/periodic, not server-pushed (no FCM), so a backgrounded app may be up to 15 minutes behind.
3. No refresh-session management UI (you cannot list/revoke other devices), and a revoked refresh token means signing in again.
4. No E2EE and no database encryption at rest — unchanged, as instructed. No calling work started.
5. Emulator was shut down after the run; the AVD and AEHD driver remain installed for future runs.

## Part 2 — E2EE architecture and proposals (design only, nothing implemented)

Delivered (uncommitted, awaiting your approval):

| File | Contents |
|---|---|
| `E2EE_ARCHITECTURE.md` | Library evaluation, PQXDH + Double Ratchet, per-device sessions, envelope v2 wire format, multi-device fan-out, attachments, at-rest plan, compatibility, acceptance criteria |
| `KEY_MANAGEMENT.md` | Key inventory, generation/storage, rotation schedule, verification, backup options (none / passphrase archive / QR device linking), lost-device revocation, compromise recovery |
| `THREAT_MODEL.md` | Assets, 9 adversaries, what is/isn't protected, metadata leakage, residual risks, threat→test mapping |
| `E2EE_IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` | Server schema v2→v3 and Room v1→v2 migration DDL, Android module/integration proposal, 15-case two-phone test plan plus rollout/rollback |
| `SECURITY.md` (updated) | New "designed, not implemented" section; device-verification results; explicit `endToEndEncryptionImplemented = false` until criteria are met |
| `README.md` (updated) | Doc table, refreshed device rows, corrected stale "not run"/"no on-device proof" claims |

**Recommendation: libsignal (`org.signal:libsignal-android`)** — the only maintained Android-packaged implementation of PQXDH (Kyber1024 + X25519) and Double Ratchet, with per-device addressing and prekey/Kyber stores, 0.103.x–0.106.x released through late 2026, native libs for all four Android ABIs.

**Licence gate that needs your decision:** libsignal is **AGPL-3.0-only**, so a distributed KONNEX becomes an AGPL combined work. If KONNEX must stay proprietary, the fallback is **vodozemac (Apache-2.0)** — active, but no PQXDH and it needs our own Rust/UniFFI Android build. OpenMLS (MIT) is noted as the group-messaging path, not v1. Deprecated/legacy options (`libolm`, `libsignal-protocol-java`) are explicitly excluded. Your 2026 phone set matters here: Android 9 has no hardware Curve25519, which is why keys are wrapped with a Keystore AES key rather than expected from KeyStore.

Design guarantees written down: server stores only opaque envelopes (never bodies or attachment keys), per-file AES-256-GCM attachment keys travel inside the message, TOFU + safety numbers with a hard block on identity change, and honest limits (social-graph/timestamp metadata visible; a malicious server can withhold or replay; unlocked-device compromise is out of scope; SQLCipher is required before any at-rest claim).

No messaging code was changed, no dependencies added, and no E2EE claim is made anywhere. The proposal stops here for approval on: **licence choice**, SQLCipher scope, 1:1-only v1, and backup model. Say which way you want to go and I'll start with the flagged crypto module and the migration tests.

## E2EE implementation readiness — evaluation and proposal complete

No code, dependency, schema change or protocol change was made. Everything below is documentation awaiting your approval.

### 1. Library verdict

**libsignal** is the recommendation: it is the only maintained option with **PQXDH (Kyber1024 + X25519)** *and* **Double Ratchet**, official Android AAR (minSdk 23, four ABIs), and 0.103–0.106 releases through late 2026. Blocking conditions, stated plainly:

- **Licence:** declared AGPL-3.0-only in its POM. A distributed KONNEX becomes an AGPL combined work and must publish source. **The repo currently has no `LICENSE`/`NOTICE` file at all** — this must be resolved first. No commercial licence exists for libsignal.
- **Build risk:** the AAR is compiled to **Java 21** bytecode with desugaring; this build runs **JDK 17 / AGP 8.7.3**, so D8's acceptance of class-file v65 must be verified (V-1).
- **Fallback:** **vodozemac** (Apache-2.0) — real Double Ratchet, but **no PQXDH and no Kyber**: Olm's triple-DH handshake is explicitly *not* equivalent to Signal's PQXDH, and there is no official standalone Android artifact, so KONNEX would own a Rust/UniFFI build pipeline.
- **OpenMLS** (MIT) is documented as the future group path: MLS is epoch/tree-ratcheted, not Double Ratchet, and standard ciphersuites are not post-quantum.
- Rejected with reasons: libolm (deprecated 2024), libsignal-protocol-java (GPL, unmaintained), primitives-only libraries (would require designing a protocol ourselves), Proteus, OpenPGP.

Audit status is reported as found: protocol-level academic analyses exist for X3DH/Double Ratchet/PQXDH; **no complete public third-party audit of the libsignal implementation was found**; libolm had a 2016 NCC audit, vodozemac none that I could confirm.

### 2. Database encryption

SQLCipher Community (BSD-style) via Room `SupportOpenHelperFactory`; 32-byte random DB key in SQLCipher **raw-key** form, wrapped by a non-exportable Keystore AES-256-GCM key and stored outside the DB. Migration is export → `cipher_integrity_check` + `integrity_check` + row-count comparison → atomic swap with `.plain.bak` retained three verified opens → cleanup; a marker outside the DB makes every interruption point resumable or rollbackable. Includes WAL checkpointing to avoid plaintext residue, startup `cipher_version` assertion, and a rule that the plaintext DB is never deleted before a verified encrypted open.

**Decision needed:** current SQLCipher 4.20 pairs with `androidx.sqlite` 2.7/Room 3, while this project pins **Room 2.6.1**; either pin an older SQLCipher or schedule a Room upgrade milestone — `AGENTS.md` forbids a casual bump.

### 3. E2EE v1 scope

1:1 only, independent device identity, PQXDH session establishment, Double Ratchet (forward secrecy + post-compromise recovery), AEAD authentication, QR/safety-number verification, hard block on identity change, ciphertext-only server, per-file AES-GCM attachment keys. Multi-device is **prepared** (`deviceId` in schema, per-device envelopes, fan-out diagrams) but explicitly listed as deferred and not claimed. Wire format gains `protocolVersion` (1 = plaintext today, 2 = envelope), with capability advertisement and downgrade protection.

### 4. Backups

Streaming AES-256-GCM container: per-backup DEK wrapped by an Argon2id (64 MiB, t=3) passphrase KEK **and/or** a 160-bit recovery key via HKDF — so either unlocks, and changing a passphrase rewraps 48 bytes instead of re-encrypting the file. Backup keys are provably independent of identity keys, ratchet sessions and the SQLCipher key. Destinations: local SAF, Google Drive, NAS/SMB, WebDAV, SFTP, private KONNEX server — all sealed before upload; unconfigured destinations return `NotConfigured` instead of faking success. Restoring identity keys is off by default.

## Database encryption readiness — audit complete, no code touched

New document: **`DATABASE_ENCRYPTION_IMPLEMENTATION_READINESS.md`** (503 lines) — findings, exact versions, per-file change list, state machine, failure matrix, security implications, 20 test cases, rollback, blockers, and a sign-off checklist.

### Answer to the central question

**Yes — SQLCipher works with Room 2.6.1 without upgrading Room**, by pinning:

```toml
net.zetetic:sqlcipher-android:4.13.0
```

Verified from POMs, not assumed: Room 2.6.1 requires `androidx.sqlite:sqlite:2.4.0`; SQLCipher 4.13.0 declares `2.2.0`, so Gradle resolves up to 2.4.0 and nothing moves. **4.14–4.17 force `sqlite` 2.6.2 and 4.18+ force 2.7.0 (Room 3)** — that is exactly why "SQLCipher 4.20 is compatible" is false for this project. Corroborated by Zetetic issue #81: Room 2.6.1 + SQLCipher built on sqlite 2.2 works; Room 2.8.4 crashes because SQLCipher lacks `beginTransactionReadOnly()`.

Also verified: 16 KB page support since 4.6.1 (Play requirement), ABIs `arm64-v8a/armeabi-v7a/x86/x86_64`, Community licence BSD-style, latest release 4.20.0 (2026-10-27) vs 4.13.0 (2026-01-20).

### Repository findings that change the plan

1. **The DB is a lazy process-wide singleton opened from a startup coroutine** (`AppContainer.database` → `KonnexApplication.onCreate`), and WorkManager **auto-initializes** (`androidx.startup.InitializationProvider` confirmed in the merged manifest) — so `SyncWorker`/`BackupWorker` can open the DB in a fresh process with no UI. Migration must therefore run **inside the first DB open**, behind a gate; a splash-screen migration alone is insufficient.
2. **No migrations exist yet** (Room v1, one exported schema, no destructive fallback) and there is **no raw SQLite/file access** anywhere — one builder call to change.
3. 9 entities / 9 DAOs, 15 DB consumers, 6 `withTransaction` call sites, all going through `RoomDatabase` → unaffected if the factory is wired once.
4. **`AndroidKeystoreCipher` only handles Strings** — it needs a byte-array wrap (or base64 reuse) plus an AAD-bound key for the DB key; today there is no rotation API.
5. **Backups are an unencrypted ZIP containing message bodies.** DB encryption would not protect them; that gap is now called out as a release condition, not a footnote.
6. Attachments live as plaintext files in `filesDir/attachments` — outside this milestone's coverage, also stated.

### Failure cases added beyond the earlier proposal

Keystore key **missing** vs **permanently invalidated** (separate paths), disk-full before rename, marker-lost-but-files-present (adopt state by content sniffing), `.bak` + encrypted DB both valid, double migration attempts, downgrade to a pre-SQLCipher APK (unreadable DB), worker-starts-before-migration, and the deliberate plaintext window — tightened from "keep `.plain.bak` for 3 opens" to **delete immediately after the first verified encrypted open**, since a lingering plaintext copy is worse than a rollback that user backup can cover.

### Remaining blockers before coding

1. **SQLCipher 4.13.x support window** — it is ten months behind 4.20; either confirm Zetetic still ships fixes for it, or approve 4.14.1 + the `sqlite` 2.6.2 upgrade with full Room regression. This is the one item I could not settle from public sources.
2. Raw-key pass-through (`x'…'`) in `SupportOpenHelperFactory` 4.13.0 — must be proven by test D1, with passphrase-KDF fallback.

4. Approval of a blocking migration UX and the plaintext-window policy.
5. Acknowledgement that backups and attachments remain unprotected until their own milestones.

The approval checklist is §11 of the document — 15 items, ending with the explicit go-ahead to implement. I'm stopping here: no SQLCipher dependency, no code, no migration, no commit.

## Verification gate: **NO-GO on 4.13.0** — conditional GO on 4.17.0 after a dependency spike

New report: **`SQLCIPHER_SECURITY_VERIFICATION.md`** (428 lines). No code, Gradle, schema, phone or commit changed. The previous readiness doc now carries a one-line "superseded on version choice" note; its audit and state machine remain current.

### The finding that changes the plan

Zetetic's 4.14.0 release notes state: SQLite is updated to 3.51.3, *"which fixes a critical WAL-reset database corruption bug. Applications running SQLCipher in WAL mode are strongly advised to upgrade."* **4.13.0 ships SQLite 3.51.2 — before that fix — and Room uses WAL by default.** Combined with Zetetic's support model (no Community LTS or backports; dedicated maintenance is a paid entitlement), the earlier 4.13.0 pin is not defensible.

### Version assessment

| | 4.13.0 | 4.14.1 | 4.17.0 | 4.20.0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SQLite | 3.51.2 | 3.51.3 | 3.53.3 | 3.54.1 |
| WAL corruption fix | **No** | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `sqlcipher_export` sanitization | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| 4.19 advisory fixes | No | No | No | Yes |
| `androidx.sqlite` | 2.2.0 | 2.6.2 | 2.6.2 | 2.7.0 |
| Verdict | **rejected** | floor | **recommended, conditional** | after G0 |

**Recommended pin: `net.zetetic:sqlcipher-android:4.17.0`** — highest version on the `androidx.sqlite 2.6.2` line, and the fixes that matter for this codebase. Room stays 2.6.1, but `androidx.sqlite` must move 2.4.0 → 2.6.2, which pulls `sqlite-framework`, `sqlite-bundled`, `sqlite-ktx` and `kotlin-stdlib 2.1.20`.

### Raw-key verification

The Java layer passes the caller's `byte[]` **unchanged** to `nativeKey(connectionPtr, password)` — no encoding, quoting, hashing or KDF (`SupportOpenHelperFactory` and `SQLiteConnection` source read). Zetetic's API docs define `x'<64 hex>'` as a **raw 32-byte key with no key derivation**, and 96 hex as key + salt. So the intended design is supported. The JNI C shim itself was not read, so this is **partially verified**, with a non-destructive R1 test design (dedicated test DB name, header check, wrong-key check, raw-binary control) in §3.3.

### Native and packaging (measured, not assumed)

Downloaded and inspected the actual AARs:

- **One `.so` per ABI**, no `libcrypto`/`libssl` — LibTomCrypt is static, so no OpenSSL duplication.
- **16 KB pages verified from ELF headers**: every `PT_LOAD` has `p_align = 0x4000` on arm64-v8a, armeabi-v7a and x86_64.
- **Size**: AAR 4.01 MB; arm64 `.so` 2.10 MB (≈ +2.1 MB per install), universal ≈ +7.6 MB.
- **R8**: `proguard.txt` ships keep rules for `net.zetetic.database.**`, native methods and annotations.
- **Bytecode**: Java 17 (class major 61), matching the project toolchain.

### Migration safety verdict

Structure is sound; four hard changes are required:

1. **WAL is the dangerous part**: checkpoint → assert 0-byte WAL → delete `-wal`/`-shm` **before and after** the swap, or plaintext pages survive the migration.
2. **Deleting `.plain.bak` after the first encrypted open is insufficient.** Replace with a two-launch checkpoint: open + `cipher_integrity_check` + `quick_check` + row-count receipt → `CONFIRMED_PENDING_RESTART` → next cold start re-verifies → only then delete.
3. **Worker gating**: WorkManager auto-init is confirmed in the merged manifest, so `SyncWorker`/`BackupWorker` must return `Result.retry()` while migration is not `DONE`, in addition to the DB-open mutex.
4. **Startup ordering**: migration must precede the `KonnexApplication` coroutine that already touches the DB, with the UI shown before it blocks.

### Backup / attachment gates

Backups are currently a **plaintext ZIP with message bodies**, and attachments are **plaintext files** in `filesDir/attachments`. Six release gates in §6 prevent any "encrypted at rest" claim until those are covered or the claim is narrowed to "database only".

### Still unresolved (not dressed up as verified)

- Kotlin 2.0.21 reading Kotlin 2.1.20 metadata from `androidx.sqlite 2.6.2`.
- Room 2.6.1 runtime against `sqlite-framework 2.6.2`.
- Whether `sqlite-bundled` adds a second native SQLite to the APK.
- JNI C shim behaviour for `x'…'`.
- Real performance on the API-28 phone; OEM rename/fsync behaviour.
- Whether 4.20 + sqlite 2.7.0 is viable.

All six are itemised in §8 as U1–U10.

### Gate before implementation — G0 (not run)

An isolated probe module or throwaway branch: add 4.17.0 only there, run `:app:assembleDebug` on Kotlin 2.0.21 / AGP 8.7.3 / Room 2.6.1, record resolved versions, run R1 against a test-only DB, and inspect the APK for duplicate `.so` sets and size delta. **If G0 fails, the project must choose** between upgrading Kotlin/AGP/androidx as its own milestone, a different encryption approach, or accepting an unsupported library — none of which I recommend silently.

### Current state

- Working tree: documentation only (`README.md`, `SECURITY.md` modified earlier; 10 untracked docs including this one). No build file, Kotlin file or schema touched.
- Both phones still have `com.konnex.debug` installed; nothing installed, removed or reset.
- Nothing committed; HEAD still `0ba0c2c`.

The approval checklist is §9 of the report — blocking items are G0, accepting the `androidx.sqlite 2.6.2` move, the 4.17.0 pin (and its gap vs 4.19/4.20), the two-launch plaintext-deletion checkpoint, WAL handling, worker gating, the backup/attachment release gates, and the downgrade policy. Implementation starts only on your explicit go-ahead.

### Why 4.20.0 is not the answer

`sqlcipher-android:4.20.0` failed AAR metadata:

> requires … compile against version **36** or later … maximum recommended compile SDK for AGP 8.7.3 is 35

The 4.18 release notes state compileSdk 37 for that line, so **4.18–4.20 are incompatible with the pinned toolchain**. 4.17.0 is the highest release that works with Room 2.6.1 / AGP 8.7.3 / Kotlin 2.0.21 — a ceiling, not a preference.

**Residual risk of 4.17.0:** it lacks the 4.19 advisory fixes (unquoted `sqlcipher_export` aliases, invalid `hexkey` URI) and 4.20's maintenance changes. The export advisory is not exploitable here **provided `sqlcipher_export` is only ever called with constant aliases** — that must be a code-review invariant. FTS5 CVEs are already fixed in 4.17 (SQLite 3.53.3); KONNEX uses no FTS.

- Minified **runtime** open (R8 build compiles; DB not opened in it).
- Performance on the API-28 phone.
- Plaintext backups and attachments remain the release-gate gaps from the previous phase.

# Next Task: SQLCipher Migration Failure-Injection & Production Readiness

The SQLCipher G0 compatibility gate has passed.

Approved technical baseline for investigation:

- SQLCipher: `net.zetetic:sqlcipher-android:4.17.0`
- Room: `2.6.1`
- androidx.sqlite: `2.6.2`
- Kotlin: `2.0.21`
- AGP: `8.7.3`
- JDK: `17`

## Mission

Design and validate the complete plaintext SQLite → encrypted SQLCipher migration lifecycle before production implementation.

**This is an investigation and test-design task, NOT implementation.**

## Strict safety constraints

1. Do not modify production Kotlin/Java source.
2. Do not modify Gradle files, dependency versions, Room entities or schemas.

- Initial plaintext database.
- Migration requested.
- WAL checkpoint.
- Plaintext database export.
- Encrypted database creation.
- Integrity verification.
- Atomic replacement.
- First verified encrypted launch.
- Second cold-start verification.
- Plaintext backup deletion.
- Migration complete.

For every transition document:

- Preconditions.
- Files involved.
- Atomicity guarantees.
- Recovery action.
- User-visible state.
- Whether retry is safe.

4. Process death during encryption.

Use synthetic data and deterministic failure injection.

## Verdict: **CONDITIONAL GO** — report at `SQLCIPHER_MIGRATION_FAILURE_INJECTION_REPORT.md`

The migration design survived every failure I could actually inject. No tested failure lost a row, and none produced a silent plaintext fallback.

### What was actually executed (not just designed)

I built a disposable probe at `.logs/m1-probe/` and ran it against synthetic data only.

**18-test migration suite: 18/18 pass on API 35, and 18/18 again on API 28.** Covers happy path, wrong key, corrupt temp, stale WAL, missing Keystore key, downgrade, both-copies-valid, gate, two migrators, and 5 crash-point recoveries.

**Real process death, five times** — `Process.killProcess`/`halt`, then recovery in a fresh process:

| Killed at | Recovery |
|---|---|
| during checkpoint | DONE, 120 rows |
| mid-export (after first encrypted byte) | DONE, 300 rows |
| after encrypted rename | DONE, 140 rows, `.bak` deleted |
| during post-swap marker write | DONE, 110 rows |
| after marker SWAPPED | DONE, 130 rows |

**Real disk full:** 6 MB tmpfs inside the probe's own files dir, 3 MB database → `database or disk is full (code 1)`. Plaintext sha unchanged, 3 000 rows still readable, temp deleted.

**Device reboot mid-migration:** reboot 2 s into a 50 MB export (~6.4 s measured) → recovery DONE, 49 000 rows. Caveat: I could not capture the marker immediately before the reboot (adb shell wedged), so "mid-export" rests on timing, not a marker snapshot.

**Concurrency:** second migrator returns `ALREADY_RUNNING` both in-process and from a second `:mig` process; a worker blocks on the gate for 1 416 ms rather than opening anything.

**API 28 (isolated `konnex_api28` emulator, Android 9):** native load, `cipher_version=4.17.0`, Room create/insert/reopen (201 rows), WAL, both integrity checks, Keystore wrap/unwrap — 9/9 smoke+Keystore, plus the full migration suite 18/18. The physical LG-G710 was **not** touched.

**Keystore:** AES-256 non-exportable (`getEncoded() == null`), AAD mismatch and single-byte tamper both fail `AEADBadTagException`, key file holds only `keyId`+wrapped blob, missing/replaced alias → typed `MISSING_ALIAS`/`UNWRAP_FAILED`.

### Performance (x86_64 API 35 emulator, synthetic)

| Nominal | real bytes | migration | throughput | peak temp | mem | encrypted open |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 10 MB | 13.9 MB | 1 658 ms | 8.0 MB/s | 27.8 MB | 13.4 MB | 26 ms |
| 50 MB | 68.2 MB | 6 411 ms | 10.1 MB/s | 136 MB | 14.3 MB | 36 ms |
| 100 MB | 134.9 MB | 12 809 ms | 10.0 MB/s | 269 MB | 13.3 MB | 63 ms |
| 250 MB | 336.6 MB | 31 241 ms | 10.3 MB/s | 672 MB | 14.7 MB | 92 ms |

Peak temp ≈ 2× database size; memory stays flat. These are emulator numbers — the report says explicitly not to extrapolate to the LG-G710.

### Conditions before coding

1. Physical API 28 phone still untested (installs were prohibited); emulator passed.
2. `.plain.bak` must die in the same launch after the first verified encrypted open.
3. Keystore **invalidation is only mapped** — the real `KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException` trigger needs biometric enrollment/lock change; auth-bound key creation is refused by the platform without one (`At least one fingerprint/biometric must be enrolled…`).
4. Attachments and backup payloads remain plaintext — proven on disk. The app must not claim full at-rest encryption until those ship.

Also unresolved: reboot during the two renames (killed at those points, not actually rebooted), R8 runtime, real Keystore on OEM hardware, 4.19 export-alias advisory.

**Verdict: crypto core passes; release is blocked by two High findings.**

**High**
1. **Database-unavailable crashes the app.** With the key file deleted (or its wrapped value corrupted), startup logs `KEY_MISSING`/`UNAVAILABLE`, then composition accesses `profileRepository` → `AppContainer.database` and throws on the main thread: `FATAL EXCEPTION: main … DatabaseSecurityException`. No recovery screen, no typed UI state, no export/reset path. Restoring the key file brought the data back intact.
2. **Downgrade split-brain.** Pre-Phase-1 APK → launch created a plaintext `konnex.db` while leaving `konnex-encrypted.db` untouched. Reinstalling Phase 1 then preferred the legacy file, silently running plaintext and hiding the encrypted data. Deleting the synthetic legacy DB restored the encrypted data. There is no dual-file guard; this also re-enables plaintext storage.

**Medium**
- No recoverable backup/export: `allowBackup=false` is correct, but the Keystore alias is install-bound, so restore always ends in `MISSING_ALIAS`.
- Raw key is copied into an immutable hex `String` and never zeroized.
- `SecurityInspector` swallows open failures; Settings/Profile then display **"Planned — not implemented"/"Planned"** on a broken encrypted install.

**Low:** key-creation race (not reachable with today's single container), imprecise error typing (malformed Base64 → `UNAVAILABLE`; replaced DB → `VERIFICATION_FAILED`; Keystore unavailable → `MISSING_ALIAS`), failed fresh creation leaves `-wal`/`-shm`, rename fallback can delete a valid key, unused key-file version/no rotation, global `DatabaseAccess` state, leftover wrapped test key files.

**Verified good:** 32-byte random key, non-exportable AES-256-GCM wrapping with identity AAD, distinct alias from the secret store, no raw key storage, typed refusal on missing/wrong/corrupt key, plaintext-at-encrypted-path refusal, encrypted WAL/SHM with no plaintext body, `allowBackup=false`, no key material in logcat, v2→v3 update preserving key and data, truncated APK update rejected with the app intact.

**Compatibility matrix:** Phase1→legacy unsafe (creates plaintext shadow); legacy→Phase1 unsafe (split-brain); Phase1→newer Phase1 safe; interrupted update safe; missing key fail-closed but crashes; replaced encrypted DB fail-closed but mis-typed. Recommendation: do not ship Phase 1; minimum safe release is the build containing the dual-file guard and availability gate, ideally with server-side minimum-client enforcement.

- `DatabaseBootstrap` now checks both `konnex.db` and `konnex-encrypted.db` first and fails closed with `AMBIGUOUS_DATABASES`, opening/deleting neither.
- Verified: legacy-only → hardened works normally; hardened → legacy creates plaintext; re-upgrade shows "Two local databases found" with both files and the key preserved. Repeated the full cycle twice; deleting the synthetic shadow restores the encrypted data.

**Medium/low fixes**
- Malformed Base64/envelope/version → `KEY_CORRUPTED`; wrong/replaced database → `DATABASE_CORRUPTED`; Keystore alias loss vs provider failure distinguished.
- `SecurityInspector` no longer touches or swallows the database; Settings/Profile show Enabled / Legacy plaintext / Unavailable / Checking instead of "Planned".
- Raw-key literal built as bytes (no immutable hex `String`); raw key zeroed after spec creation.
- Key creation uses a JVM lock + OS file lock + atomic publish; failed fresh creation cleans `-wal`/`-shm`/`-journal`; key-file version validated; test key artifacts cleaned up.
- No key rotation or speculative recovery mechanism added.

- Truncated/interrupted update rejected; installed version stayed intact.

## Phase 2.2 implemented

Encrypted backups now use a versioned `KONNXBK2` container:

- AES-256-GCM with 64 KiB chunks, unique nonces, authenticated chunk order/final markers, and an encrypted footer binding plaintext length, chunk count and SHA-256.
- One random 32-byte DEK per backup, independently wrapped by an Argon2id passphrase KEK (64 MiB, t=3, p=1) and an HKDF-SHA256 key derived from a 160-bit recovery key.
- The header core is authenticated as AAD in every chunk, footer and wrap slot.
- Passphrase change and recovery rotation rewrite only a 64-byte wrapped-DEK slot; the encrypted body remains byte-identical.
- Restore authenticates the entire container before parsing the ZIP, validates schema/counts/IDs/FKs, and imports in one Room transaction.
- Scheduled backups use a recovery key sealed under Keystore alias `konnex.backup.recovery.v1`; the passphrase is never stored.
- The inner ZIP remains in memory only. It is never written to disk or passed to a storage provider.

I also fixed three review findings after the first green run: restore now wipes its backing buffer directly, repeated rewraps use bounded unique object names, and the Keystore save path wipes sealed bytes on every outcome.

## Phase 2.3 complete — attachment encryption at rest

Implemented end-to-end local attachment encryption, resumable plaintext migration, encrypted-backup integration, a streaming content provider, documentation, and verification. **No commit was made.**

### Encryption architecture

- **Tink streaming AEAD** `AES256_GCM_HKDF_4KB` (AES-256-GCM with HKDF-SHA256 and 4 KiB segments). No custom cipher or framing.
- **One independent random Tink keyset per attachment**; never shared with SQLCipher, backups, other attachments, or tokens.
- Keysets are wrapped with a dedicated non-exportable Keystore key, alias **`konnex.attachment.wrap.v1`**.
- Files: `files/attachments/<id>.konnexatt` plus `<id>.konnexatt.key`.
- **16-byte versioned header** `KONNXAT1` / version 1 / algorithm 1 / flags 0.
- Header plus `(attachmentId, ownerId, formatVersion, mimeType)` is authenticated as Tink AAD. The key sidecar is wrapped with the same metadata under a separate key-AAD tag.
- Incremental 64 KiB processing; temp file → fsync → atomic move. Plaintext attachments are never written to persistent storage.
- `read()` is limited to 32 MiB in memory; larger data uses `openDecrypted()` streaming.
- Legacy plaintext paths are rejected; there is **no plaintext fallback**.
- Read-only, non-exported `AttachmentContentProvider` streams decrypted bytes through a pipe under a per-URI grant.

### Migration and recovery

`AttachmentMigration` runs at startup before normal work:

1. Process semaphore + cross-process file lock.
2. Durable journal under `noBackupFilesDir`, atomically rewritten at every phase.
3. Preflight duplicate paths, root containment, size/SHA-256, and free-space check.
4. Generate/install the wrapped key sidecar.
5. Stream-encrypt to temp, fsync, verify plaintext digest.
6. Authenticate the encrypted temp file and compare against the row.
7. Atomically install ciphertext, update the Room path.
8. Delete plaintext only after verification and row update.
9. Resume interrupted cleanup by re-verifying the ciphertext.
10. Surface explicit `KEY_UNAVAILABLE`, `LOW_STORAGE`, or `RECOVERY_REQUIRED` states. Corrupt/duplicate/out-of-root/orphan cases preserve originals.

A final-review fix now also validates an already-encrypted row’s key sidecar, so a missing key cannot be reported as “Enabled.”

### Backup integration

- Phase 2.2 container is unchanged; inner archive schema is now **2** (schema 1 still restores).
- Encrypted attachment ciphertext and raw Tink keysets are stored **inside** the authenticated `KONNXBK2` container.
- Attachment keys remain independent of backup DEK/KEK, SQLCipher, and other attachments.
- Restore unwraps in memory, generates a fresh local key, re-encrypts for the target owner, verifies size/SHA-256, then imports. No plaintext attachment reaches disk.
- Missing/corrupt attachments are skipped or marked failed without aborting message restore.

### Remaining limitations

- **Not E2EE and not server-side encryption.** Server-held attachment blobs and the server database remain plaintext.
- **Unlocked-device malware** can read decrypted streams; at-rest encryption only protects the locked/offline file state.
- **Backup attachment packaging is memory-bound**: 256 MiB per attachment entry, 1 GiB archive cap. Storage crypto streams; backup export/restore does not fully.
- **Migration crash recovery is fault-injected** at nine journal checkpoints, not a real OS process kill. Low storage is injected, not a real ENOSPC.
- **No share UI** obtains a URI grant; provider behavior is tested directly, not against a third-party app.
- No thumbnail/image cache exists; a future one must reuse the encrypted path.
- **Emulator-only evidence**; physical phones were untouched. The R8 APK was built, not installed/run.
- No independent cryptographic review.

   - Existing profile, conversations, messages, contacts and attachment rows are preserved.
   - Old archives are additive only.
   - Duplicate restored attachment files are deleted after the DB transaction.

4. **Security-panel truthfulness**
   - `secretsEncryptedAtRest` now reflects actual Keystore availability instead of always reporting `true`.

# Phase 2.5 — Fresh Installation Backup Recovery

Phase 2.4 identified F-04 (High): a fresh KONNEX installation cannot restore an existing encrypted backup because restore currently depends on a local backup\_records entry.

Implement a complete, secure backup recovery workflow.

## 1\. Initial audit

Inspect the existing:

- KONNXBK2 encrypted container.
- Argon2id passphrase unlock.
- 160-bit recovery-key mechanism.
- Backup credential storage.
- Restore engine and archive validation.
- Attachment encryption and re-encryption.
- Database availability and migration gates.
- Compose navigation and settings UI.

Preserve the existing backup format unless a justified compatibility change is necessary.

## 2\. Fresh-install recovery

Allow users to restore from:

- A local SAF document URI.
- An externally supplied encrypted backup file.
- A supported configured remote storage destination.

Do not require a pre-existing local backup record.

Support both independent unlock methods:

- Backup passphrase.
- Recovery key.

Never transmit passphrases or recovery keys to the server.

## 3\. Recovery workflow

Implement the following sequence:

1. Select an encrypted backup.
2. Inspect and validate its public header.
3. Identify supported format and version.
4. Request the appropriate unlock credential.
5. Authenticate the container.
6. Validate archive structure and integrity.
7. Display a restore summary.
8. Require explicit user confirmation.
9. Restore database data transactionally.
10. Re-encrypt attachments using fresh local Keystore-backed keys.
11. Verify restored data and attachment references.
12. Report success or a typed recoverable failure.

Never write decrypted archive contents to persistent plaintext storage.

## 4\. Security and recovery behavior

Handle:

- Wrong passphrase.
- Invalid recovery key.
- Corrupt or truncated container.
- Unsupported backup version.
- Missing attachment blobs.
- Missing or invalid Keystore aliases.
- Insufficient storage.
- Process death during restore.
- Repeated restore attempts.
- Existing local data.
- Interrupted database migration.
- Downgrade and upgrade scenarios.

Do not overwrite newer local data silently.

Do not generate replacement device identities when existing identity material is unavailable.

## 5\. Restore safety

Use a staging strategy and persistent recovery journal.

The original application data must remain recoverable until the restored state has been independently verified.

Ensure attachment files and database references cannot become inconsistent.

Do not expose a success state before all required verification completes.

## 6\. UI

Implement a real Compose recovery flow.

Include:

- Select backup.
- Passphrase/recovery-key entry.
- Backup inspection.
- Restore preview.
- Confirmation.
- Progress.
- Recoverable errors.
- Completion summary.

Do not expose credentials in logs, saved state or analytics.

## What was built

**Fresh-install recovery engine** (`BackupRecoveryEngine`) that never touches `backup_records`:
- **Sources:** a SAF document the user picks (`ActivityResultContracts.OpenDocument`) or any `.konnexbackup` discovered in a configured, readable destination (`provider.list("konnex-backups")`).
- **Two unlock methods:** passphrase (Argon2id) or the 160-bit recovery key (HKDF) — exactly one, and only the slot the container actually has. Credentials are wiped after every step and never persisted, logged, or sent anywhere.
- **New container primitive:** `EncryptedBackupContainer.checkCredential` unwraps the DEK and wipes it without walking the body, so "wrong passphrase" and "damaged container" become distinct typed outcomes (`WRONG_CREDENTIAL` / `INVALID_RECOVERY_KEY` vs `CORRUPT_CONTAINER`). Format, AADs and limits are unchanged — existing `KONNXBK2` backups stay valid.
- **Flow:** stage → inspect public header → unlock/authenticate → verify every chunk+footer → parse/validate archive → preview (counts, attachment coverage, local conflicts) → explicit confirmation bound to the container's SHA-256 fingerprint → re-authenticate → re-encrypt attachments under fresh local keys → one Room transaction with in-transaction read-back → decrypt every restored attachment again to verify → typed result.
- **Crash safety:** non-secret `restore-journal.json` (fsync + atomic replace, phases `STAGED`/`PREPARED`/`ATTACHMENTS_WRITTEN`/`COMMITTING`/`COMMITTED`/`FAILED`), an OS `FileLock` (`restore.lock`), and `recoverInterrupted()` which deletes `-restored-` files no row references. A crash can leave extra files but never a row pointing at a missing file, and success is never reported before verification.
- **Compose flow:** select → credential entry → preview → progress with typed step labels → completion summary, with typed errors and retry to the failing step. Entry point added to Backup settings so it exists on a new install.

Also fixed a real reporting defect found by the new tests: `RestoreReport.missingAttachments` always reported 0 because it queried the table after inserting the `MISSING` row (Medium, now counted against what the archive actually carried).

# Phase 2.6 — Streaming Backup & Restore (Production Hardening)

Implement Phase 2.6 of KONNEX: eliminate memory-bound backup and restore operations while preserving the existing encryption architecture, backup compatibility, database integrity, and crash-recovery guarantees.

This is a production security and reliability task. Audit the actual repository before making changes. Do not assume that previous phase reports accurately describe the current implementation.

## 1\. Initial Audit — Mandatory

Before implementation, inspect:

- `EncryptedBackupContainer.kt`
- `BackupEngineImpl.kt`
- `BackupRecoveryEngineImpl.kt`
- `BackupArchive.kt`
- `RoomBackupDataSource.kt`
- `RestoreJournal.kt`
- `RestoreProcessLock.kt`
- `LocalAttachmentStore.kt`
- `AttachmentStorageGate.kt`
- All backup storage providers and SAF integration.
- All backup-related Compose screens and state holders.
- Existing migration, database availability, and worker coordination.

Trace every production allocation and I/O path.

Identify:

- Full-container byte arrays.
- Full ZIP/archive materialization.
- Full attachment materialization.
- Temporary plaintext files.
- Unbounded buffers.
- Duplicate copies of encrypted or decrypted data.
- Restore transaction memory usage.
- Existing journal and recovery guarantees.

Write an audit report before implementation.

## 2\. Streaming Encrypted Container

Preserve the existing `KONNXBK2` format and backward compatibility.

Implement streaming APIs for:

- Container creation.
- Container authentication.
- Container decryption.
- Credential verification.
- Container inspection.
- Passphrase rewrapping.
- Recovery-key rewrapping.

Requirements:

- AES-256-GCM.
- Existing 64 KiB chunk format.
- Existing authenticated header, chunk ordering, final markers, and footer.
- Existing Argon2id parameters and HKDF-SHA256 derivation.
- Unique nonces.
- Strict chunk ordering and truncation detection.
- Authenticate every chunk and footer before considering the container valid.
- Never expose unauthenticated plaintext to archive parsing or database import.
- Preserve existing recovery and passphrase behavior.

Do not silently introduce a new backup format.

If a format change is unavoidable, introduce an explicit new version and retain readers for existing backups.

## 3\. Streaming Backup Export

Replace the current in-memory export pipeline.

Required pipeline:

`Room data → bounded archive writer → streaming encrypted container → temporary encrypted file → verified destination`

Requirements:

- Stream attachment content instead of materializing attachment byte arrays.
- Use bounded buffers.
- Avoid writing plaintext archive files to persistent storage.
- Do not retain the complete ZIP or container in memory.
- Verify encrypted output before publishing it.
- Use temporary encrypted files and atomic publication where supported.
- Clean up incomplete files after errors.
- Preserve existing backup metadata and attachment integrity.
- Do not delete an existing valid backup if a new backup fails.

Define and enforce explicit maximum limits for:

- Individual attachment size.
- Total archive size.
- Number of archive entries.
- Entry names and metadata lengths.
- Total decompressed size.

Prevent ZIP bombs, duplicate entries, path traversal, and integer overflow.

## 4\. Streaming Restore

Replace the current memory-bound restore path.

Required pipeline:

`Selected source → encrypted container verification → authenticated streaming decryption → bounded archive parser → staging → verified Room import`

Requirements:

- Do not parse archive data before container authentication.
- Do not materialize the entire encrypted container or decrypted archive.
- Stream attachments directly into encrypted staging files.
- Never write attachment plaintext to persistent storage.
- Re-encrypt restored attachments using fresh local Tink keysets and the target device's Keystore.
- Preserve owner-bound AAD.
- Validate attachment size and SHA-256.
- Validate schema version, entity counts, IDs, relationships, and foreign keys.
- Prevent duplicate IDs and path collisions.
- Preserve additive restore semantics.
- Never roll back newer local records.

### Database consistency

Do not claim that a streaming implementation is atomic merely because it uses a Room transaction.

Evaluate whether large imports can safely fit into one transaction.

If necessary, implement a durable staged-import design with:

- Import identifier.
- Staging metadata.
- Durable journal.
- Explicit commit state.
- Recovery after process death.
- Cleanup of unreferenced staged files.
- Verification that no database row references a missing attachment.

A partially completed restore must never be reported as successful.

## 5\. Crash Recovery and Storage Safety

Extend the existing restore journal rather than creating an unrelated recovery mechanism.

Test process interruption at:

- Source staging.
- Header inspection.
- Credential verification.
- Chunk authentication.
- Archive parsing.
- Attachment staging.
- Database import.
- Database commit.
- Attachment publication.
- Final cleanup.

Requirements:

- Use atomic journal updates with fsync.
- Use cross-process file locking.
- Coordinate with `AttachmentStorageGate`.
- Preserve existing backup files.
- Never delete the only valid copy.
- Detect insufficient storage before destructive operations.
- Recover deterministically after process death and reboot.
- Distinguish retryable failures from permanent corruption.

Test real process termination where possible, not only simulated exceptions.

## 6\. Storage Provider Compatibility

Audit and test:

- Local device storage.
- Android SAF document providers.
- WebDAV.
- Google Drive.
- KONNEX server storage.

Do not claim streaming support for a provider unless its actual adapter supports streaming.

If a provider cannot support reliable streaming or atomic publication, document its limitations and fail safely.

Avoid loading remote files completely into memory.

## 7\. Performance and Memory Tests

Test with synthetic backup datasets of:

- 10 MB.
- 100 MB.
- 500 MB.
- 1 GB, if emulator storage permits.

Measure:

- Peak Java heap.
- Peak native memory where measurable.
- Export duration.
- Restore duration.
- Encryption/decryption throughput.
- Temporary disk usage.
- Number of buffer allocations.
- Garbage collection frequency.
- Recovery time after interruption.

The critical requirement is that peak application memory must remain bounded and must not grow linearly with total backup size.

Set an explicit memory budget and justify it with measurements.

Do not extrapolate emulator performance to physical devices.

## 8\. Security Requirements

Verify:

- No passphrase in files, preferences, logs, or saved state.
- No recovery key in plaintext persistent storage.
- No plaintext backup archive on disk.
- No plaintext attachment staging.
- No raw DEK persistence.
- No unauthenticated plaintext exposed to consumers.
- No downgrade to plaintext backup format.
- No silent fallback when authentication fails.
- No deletion of valid backups during failed export or restore.
- Temporary buffers containing secrets are wiped where practical.

Do not invent cryptographic primitives.

Prefer established libraries and existing tested implementations.

Document any unavoidable secret lifetime in memory.

## 9\. Testing Requirements

Add tests for:

### JVM tests

- Streaming encryption/decryption.
- Existing KONNXBK2 compatibility.
- Chunk ordering and authentication.
- Truncation and tampering.
- Wrong credentials.
- ZIP traversal and ZIP bomb protection.
- Duplicate entries.
- Integer overflow.
- Large attachments.
- Bounded-memory behavior.
- Interrupted export.
- Interrupted restore.
- Journal recovery.
- Repeated restore.
- Concurrent backup and restore.
- Concurrent attachment migration.

### Android instrumentation

Run on API 28 and API 35:

- Real Keystore-backed recovery key.
- Real SQLCipher database.
- Real Room import.
- Real encrypted attachment storage.
- SAF provider tests where feasible.
- Process-death recovery.
- Insufficient-storage behavior.
- R8/minified release compatibility.

Run existing regression suites as well.

## 10\. Regression and Compatibility

Do not break:

- SQLCipher 4.17.0.
- Room 2.6.1.
- Existing KONNXBK2 backups.
- Passphrase recovery.
- Recovery-key recovery.
- Phase 2.3 attachment encryption.
- Phase 2.4 storage coordination.

- Existing additive restore behavior.
- Existing downgrade protections.

Do not modify E2EE protocols, server authentication, database schemas, or unrelated application features unless strictly necessary.

## 13\. Final Acceptance Criteria

Phase 2.6 can only be marked complete if:

1. Backup export no longer materializes the full archive in memory.
2. Restore no longer materializes the full container or archive in memory.
3. Attachment processing is streaming.
4. Peak memory remains within a documented fixed budget.
5. Existing KONNXBK2 backups remain readable.
6. Authentication occurs before archive data is consumed.
7. Crash recovery works at the critical commit boundaries.
8. No plaintext backup or attachment staging is found.
9. API 28 and API 35 regression suites pass.
10. Debug, release, and R8 builds pass.
11. Existing security guarantees remain intact.

If any criterion cannot be verified, explicitly mark it BLOCKED or NOT VERIFIED.

Do not report simulated tests as real process-death tests.

Do not claim a provider supports streaming without testing its actual implementation.

Do not claim production readiness merely because compilation succeeds.

**Start with the repository audit. Then implement incrementally, run tests after each major component, and finish with an evidence-based report.**

Phase 2.6 is implemented, verified, and reported. Here is the evidence-based summary.

## What was built

**Streaming container** (`EncryptedBackupContainer.kt`) — `openWriter`/`StreamEncryptor` and `openReader`/`StreamDecryptor` (`readHeader`, `verifyBody`, `openPlaintext`, `read`, `finish`), all over the **unchanged KONNXBK2 byte layout** (AES-256-GCM, 64 KiB chunks, index-bound AAD, final marker, authenticated footer, same Argon2id/HKDF parameters). `verifyBody()` authenticates every chunk and the footer with the DEK before a single plaintext byte is exposed, then `openPlaintext()` re-reads with the same DEK — one Argon2 per restore. `inspect`, `verifyCredential`, both rewrap paths are streaming too; the legacy `encrypt()` now delegates, so there is one implementation of the format.

**Streaming export/restore** — new `BackupArchiveStream` writer/reader (bounded buffers, digest-per-entry, order-agnostic reading for old backups), `exportBackupFiles`/`restoreBackupFiles` in `LocalAttachmentStore`, `BackupEngineImpl` (temp encrypted file → fsync → verify → atomic publish; restore: verify → decrypt → parse → ciphertext-only staging → fresh Tink keyset re-encrypt → one chunked Room transaction), `BackupRecoveryEngineImpl` streaming `authenticate`, and WebDAV file-streaming upload/download.

**Limits** — 256 MiB/entry, 32 MiB payload, 1 MiB manifest, 64 KiB key envelope, 1 GiB total decompressed, 10 000 entries, 255-char names, `Math.addExact` throughout; traversal, duplicates, unmanifested entries and bombs rejected.

## Bugs found and fixed during verification

1. `StreamDecryptor.restart()` didn't reset `footerVerified` → every verify-then-decrypt flow failed.
2. Trailing bytes after the footer were accepted.
3. `ZipOutputStream` was being double-wrapped (nested ZIP) in the engine and instrumentation tests.
4. `BackupArchiveStreamReader` closed the plaintext stream it was handed, so the container could never be finalised — ownership now stays with the caller.

## Verification (actual results)

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| JVM `./gradlew test` | **172 tests, 0 failures** (`domain:backup` 53 → **68**, incl. 15 new streaming tests) |
| API 35 `emulator-5554` | **102 instrumentation tests, 0 failures** (stream 3, fresh 19, g1 32, g2 24, g3 24) |
| API 28 `emulator-5556` | **102 instrumentation tests, 0 failures** (same groups) |
| Real process death | `shortMsg=Process crashed.` during attachment staging; new process recovered → `OK (1 test)`, only `restore.lock` left |
| Builds | debug, debugAndroidTest, release, `-PkonnexMinifyRelease=true` (R8) all **SUCCESSFUL** |

**Memory/throughput (48 MiB attachment, measured, not extrapolated):** container 50.56 MB (0.45 % overhead); export 11.6 s / restore 23.8 s on API 35; **retained heap after GC 0 B** for restore on both APIs and 0 B / 1.47 MiB for export — constant, not proportional to payload. Budget: ≤ 32 MiB retained, ≤ 176 MiB allocation pressure.

## Honest gaps (in the report as NOT VERIFIED / PARTIAL)

100 MB/500 MB/1 GB datasets not run; native memory not measured; WebDAV streaming only mock-tested (no live server); SAF/Drive streaming partial; kill *inside* the Room import not separately tested (SQLite rollback relied on); disk-full path untested; R8 APK built but not instrumented; emulator numbers don't extrapolate to phones.

- HEAD still `1d1b98d`; **nothing committed, pushed, tagged or branched**; physical phones untouched; probes under `.logs/`; `git diff --check` clean.

Verdict in the report: streaming, bounded memory, authenticate-before-parse, format compatibility and crash recovery are verified; **production readiness is not declared** until the large-dataset, native-memory and drive/SAF items above are closed.

## 2. Đánh giá kết quả Phase 2.6

Mình đánh giá đây là một bước tiến quan trọng vì đã giải quyết được nhiều vấn đề nền tảng:

- Không còn phải nạp toàn bộ archive vào RAM.
- Giữ nguyên định dạng backup KONNXBK2.
- Xác thực container trước khi đưa dữ liệu vào archive parser.
- Streaming attachment.
- Có crash recovery bằng journal.
- Có thử nghiệm SIGKILL thật và khôi phục bằng process mới.

Đặc biệt, thử nghiệm SIGKILL là bằng chứng có giá trị hơn nhiều so với việc chỉ giả lập exception.

Tuy nhiên, mình muốn lưu ý một chi tiết kỹ thuật: báo cáo ghi nhận `verifyBody()` xác thực toàn bộ container trước rồi mới mở luồng plaintext và đọc lại. Cách này tăng độ an toàn nhưng cần tiếp tục kiểm tra việc nguồn dữ liệu có bị thay đổi giữa hai lần đọc hay không. Nên xác thực fingerprint hoặc bảo đảm nguồn bất biến trong toàn bộ quá trình.

## 2. Ba vấn đề cần lưu ý trước khi phát hành

| Vấn đề | Mức độ | Hướng xử lý |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Release dùng debug keystore | HIGH | Tạo signing identity chính thức |
| Dependency verification/locking | MEDIUM | Bổ sung kiểm soát chuỗi cung ứng |
| Immutable String chứa credentials | MEDIUM | Thiết kế giảm thời gian tồn tại secret |

Đặc biệt, lỗi ký APK bằng debug keystore phải được giải quyết trước khi phát hành thương mại.

## 3. Roadmap hiện tại

1. Phase 2.2 – 2.6
   Hoàn thành theo báo cáoBackup, encryption, recovery, streaming.

   Hoàn thành có giới hạn19 findings, 2 hardening fixes.
3. Phase 3 – E2EE

   Hoàn thiện bảo mật, ký ứng dụng, kiểm thử và phát hành.

## 4\. Bước tiếp theo: Phase 3 – E2EE

Mình khuyên không nên yêu cầu OpenCode viết ngay chức năng mã hóa tin nhắn.

Nên chia Phase 3 thành các bước:

| Phase | Nội dung |
| --- | --- |
| 3.0 | E2EE Architecture & Protocol Design |
| 3.1 | Device Identity & Key Management |
| 3.2 | One-to-One Encrypted Messaging |
| 3.3 | Multi-Device Encryption |
| 3.4 | Group Encryption |
| 3.5 | Key Rotation & Device Revocation |
| 3.6 | E2EE Security Testing |

Điểm đặc biệt quan trọng: KONNEX cần hỗ trợ nhiều thiết bị nhưng vẫn giữ nguyên quyền kiểm soát khóa của người dùng. Backup recovery không được vô tình trở thành cơ chế khiến server có thể đọc tin nhắn.

Mình đề xuất bắt đầu bằng Phase 3.0, chỉ thiết kế giao thức và threat model, chưa viết implementation. Sau khi thiết kế được kiểm tra, mới cho OpenCode triển khai từng phần.

Như vậy, chúng ta sẽ tránh phải thay đổi toàn bộ hệ thống mã hóa khi đã có nhiều người dùng và dữ liệu thật.



Tiếp theo là Phase 3.0 – E2EE Architecture & Protocol Design.

Mục tiêu của Phase này là thiết kế hoàn chỉnh nền tảng mã hóa đầu cuối cho KONNEX trước khi viết code. Đặc biệt phải giải quyết bài toán nhiều thiết bị, chat nhóm, backup, phục hồi tài khoản và quản lý khóa.

Mình chọn hướng sử dụng các giao thức mật mã đã được kiểm chứng, không tự sáng chế giao thức mới.

Định hướng Phase 3.0

- Chưa triển khai E2EE production code.
- Chưa thay đổi database schema.
- Chưa thay đổi backup format KONNXBK2.
- Chưa thay đổi server authentication.
- Thiết kế tương thích Android hiện tại và mở rộng đa nền tảng.
- Có threat model và protocol specification trước khi triển khai.

## Prompt dành cho OpenCode

Writing

# Phase 3.0 — KONNEX End-to-End Encryption Architecture & Protocol Design

Design the complete End-to-End Encryption (E2EE) architecture and protocol specification for KONNEX.

This phase establishes the cryptographic foundation for all future messaging features.

**IMPORTANT: This is a DESIGN-ONLY phase. Do not implement the production E2EE protocol yet.**

The existing KONNEX backup, encryption, storage, recovery, and Android architecture must remain intact.

The objective is to produce a technically rigorous, implementation-ready E2EE specification that can be independently reviewed before Phase 3.1 begins.

---

# 1\. Initial Repository Audit

Before designing anything, inspect the actual repository.

Review:

- Current Android application architecture.
- Domain and data modules.
- Account and authentication models.
- Device identity and installation identity.
- Existing database entities.
- Message-related models and interfaces.
- Attachment encryption.
- Android Keystore integration.
- Tink usage.
- Backup and recovery architecture.
- Multi-device assumptions.
- Server communication architecture.
- Existing networking and API contracts.
- Dependency catalog and cryptographic libraries.

Inspect all existing security documentation.

Do not assume previous phase reports accurately describe the current implementation.

Create an architecture inventory describing:

- Existing functionality.
- Missing functionality.
- Reusable components.
- Components that must remain isolated.
- Compatibility constraints.

Do not modify existing production code during the initial audit.

# 2\. E2EE Design Principles

KONNEX E2EE must follow these principles:

1. Privacy-first.
2. Zero plaintext message access for the server.
3. User-controlled cryptographic identities.
4. Independent device identities.
5. Multi-device support.
6. Secure group messaging.
7. Forward secrecy.
8. Post-compromise security where supported by the selected protocol.
9. Secure device revocation.
10. Safe key rotation.
11. Offline message delivery.
12. Cross-platform interoperability.
13. No dependence on Google Drive or any single cloud provider.
14. No custom cryptographic primitives.

The server must operate as an untrusted message relay.

The server may store encrypted message envelopes and routing metadata, but must not possess the keys required to decrypt message content.

Document unavoidable metadata leakage explicitly.

# 3\. Cryptographic Protocol Selection

Evaluate established protocols and implementations.

At minimum, investigate:

- Signal Protocol.
- X3DH and PQXDH.
- Double Ratchet.
- Sesame multi-device session management.
- MLS (Messaging Layer Security, RFC 9420).
- Established group encryption approaches.

Evaluate the suitability of:

- One-to-one conversations.
- Multi-device conversations.
- Group messaging.
- Offline delivery.
- Device revocation.
- Key rotation.
- Forward secrecy.
- Post-compromise security.
- Cross-platform support.
- Long-term maintenance.
- Licensing.
- Available audited implementations.

Do not assume every protocol is interchangeable.

Do not combine Signal and MLS primitives arbitrarily.

Select a coherent architecture with clearly defined protocol boundaries.

Provide a comparison matrix and justify the final recommendation.

Prefer maintained, established implementations over custom cryptographic code.

If a selected library has platform, licensing, or maintenance limitations, document them.

# 4\. Identity and Device Architecture

Design the complete identity model.

Distinguish:

- User account identity.
- User cryptographic identity.
- Device identity.
- Device installation identity.
- Device signing key.
- Device encryption key.
- Session keys.
- Message encryption keys.
- Group epoch keys.

Each device must have an independently verifiable cryptographic identity.

Design:

- Device registration.
- Device linking.
- Device verification.
- Device removal.
- Lost-device recovery.
- Key rotation.
- Device replacement.
- Device migration.

Define how users verify that a newly linked device actually belongs to the intended account.

The server must not be able to silently substitute device public keys.

Evaluate key transparency or equivalent mechanisms for detecting malicious key substitution.

Do not silently regenerate an existing identity after key loss.

# 5\. One-to-One Messaging Protocol

Design the full lifecycle:

1. User identity creation.
2. Device identity creation.
3. Public-key publication.
4. Prekey management.
5. Initial session establishment.
6. Message encryption.
7. Server relay.
8. Offline message storage.
9. Recipient decryption.
10. Message acknowledgement.
11. Session advancement.
12. Key rotation.
13. Device removal.

Specify:

- Message envelope structure.
- Cryptographic associated data.
- Nonce requirements.
- Message identifiers.
- Replay protection.
- Duplicate detection.
- Out-of-order delivery.
- Missing-message recovery.
- Session reset behavior.
- Authentication failure behavior.

The server must never receive plaintext messages or plaintext attachment content.

# 6\. Multi-Device Architecture

A user may own:

- Android phone.
- Android tablet.
- iPhone.
- Windows computer.
- Linux computer.

Each device must have its own cryptographic identity and sessions.

Design:

- Device directory.
- Device trust state.
- Device-to-device synchronization.
- New-device linking.
- Encrypted message fan-out.
- Device revocation.
- Offline devices.
- Removed devices receiving delayed messages.
- Device key replacement.

Do not use one shared private key copied across all devices.

Explain how historical messages become available on a newly linked device without weakening the security of existing sessions.

Distinguish:

- Message synchronization.
- Cryptographic session synchronization.
- Historical message transfer.
- Backup restoration.

# 7\. Group Messaging

Evaluate a suitable group encryption architecture.

Prefer MLS if its implementation and integration are appropriate.

Specify:

- Group creation.
- Member addition.
- Member removal.
- Membership changes.
- Epoch transitions.
- Group key management.
- Message ordering.
- Out-of-order delivery.
- Offline members.
- Group state recovery.
- Group administrator roles.
- Malicious member behavior.

Explain how a removed member loses access to future group messages.

Specify how the architecture prevents a newly added member from automatically gaining access to historical messages unless explicitly authorized.

Do not implement group encryption in this phase.

# 8\. Attachment Encryption

Design how E2EE integrates with existing attachment encryption.

Preserve the existing local attachment storage architecture.

Define:

- Per-attachment encryption keys.
- Attachment key distribution.
- Content authentication.
- Chunked media encryption.
- Attachment integrity verification.
- Thumbnail encryption.
- Attachment sharing in groups.
- Expiration and deletion.
- Key rotation.

Do not expose plaintext attachments to the server.

Do not assume the existing backup attachment encryption automatically provides E2EE.

Clearly distinguish:

- Local-at-rest encryption.
- Backup encryption.
- End-to-end attachment encryption.

# 9\. Backup and Recovery Integration

This is a critical requirement.

Design how E2EE identities and sessions interact with the existing KONNEX backup system.

Preserve:

- KONNXBK2 compatibility.
- Existing backup passphrase.
- Existing recovery key.
- Fresh-install restore.
- Streaming backup and restore.
- Android Keystore protections.

Evaluate:

- Whether identity private keys should be included in encrypted backups.
- How device-bound keys are restored on a new device.
- How to distinguish device identity recovery from account identity recovery.
- Whether historical session state should be restored.
- How to prevent backup rollback attacks.
- How to prevent stolen backups from enabling impersonation.
- How to handle lost recovery credentials.

Never allow the server to decrypt backups or recover E2EE private keys.

Do not automatically restore an old device identity onto a different device.

A restored device must undergo an explicit identity and trust procedure.

Do not modify the existing backup format in this phase.

# 10\. Server Architecture and Trust Boundaries

Design the minimum server responsibilities.

Evaluate:

- Account authentication.
- Device directory.
- Public-key distribution.
- Prekey publication.
- Prekey consumption.
- Encrypted message queues.
- Message acknowledgement.
- Device synchronization.
- Group membership coordination.
- Rate limiting.
- Abuse prevention.

Define what the server can and cannot see.

Explicitly document:

- Sender metadata.
- Recipient metadata.
- Timestamps.
- Message sizes.
- Device relationships.
- Group membership.
- Delivery status.
- IP addresses.

Do not promise perfect metadata privacy unless the architecture actually provides it.

Design defenses against:

- Public-key substitution.
- Replay.
- Duplicate prekey consumption.
- Malicious message ordering.
- Message injection.
- Device impersonation.
- Server rollback.
- Malicious server responses.

# 11\. Cross-Platform Compatibility

The protocol must be platform-independent.

Design a shared protocol layer that can eventually support:

- Android.
- iOS.
- Windows.
- Linux.

Specify:

- Canonical serialization.
- Integer and byte ordering.
- Message versioning.
- Cryptographic algorithm identifiers.
- Protocol version negotiation.
- Compatibility rules.
- Unknown-field behavior.
- Cross-platform test vectors.

Avoid platform-specific serialization of cryptographic messages.

Android Keystore may protect Android-specific private keys, but protocol messages must remain interoperable.

# 12\. Security and Threat Model

Create a detailed E2EE threat model.

Consider:

- Compromised server.
- Malicious server operator.
- Stolen device.
- Rooted Android device.
- Malware on a device.
- Malicious linked device.
- Compromised backup.
- Lost recovery key.
- Public-key substitution.
- Replay attacks.
- Session rollback.
- Malicious group member.
- Removed group member.
- Compromised cryptographic dependency.
- Malicious application update.

For each threat, document:

- Attacker capability.
- Security objective.
- Attack scenario.
- Mitigation.
- Residual risk.
- Verification strategy.

Distinguish threats that can be mitigated from those that remain outside the E2EE security boundary.

# 13\. Protocol State Machines

Provide formal state-machine specifications for:

- User identity.
- Device identity.
- Device trust.
- One-to-one sessions.
- Multi-device sessions.
- Group membership.
- Group epochs.
- Prekey lifecycle.
- Device revocation.
- Recovery.

Document valid transitions and forbidden transitions.

Include failure and recovery paths.
